lead: A scheduling algorithm chooses which ready process gets the CPU next. The four classic rules trade simplicity against average waiting time, fairness and starvation. FCFS is a plain queue. SJF gives the smallest average wait when all bursts are known. Priority scheduling ranks processes by importance. Round robin gives each process a short turn so nobody waits long. Exams ask you to draw the Gantt chart and compute average waiting time.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.6 for scheduling criteria and the preemptive/non-preemptive split, and Chapter 2.1 for the PCB fields a scheduler reads.

blocks.text: FCFS picks the process that reached the ready queue earliest. The ready queue is FIFO: the scheduler takes the head and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive.
Numbers come from the Gantt chart, the bar chart of who holds the CPU from which time to which time.
W = T − b = C − A − b,   T = C − A = W + b. For a process that runs from first dispatch to completion without preemption, W = S − A.
blocks.where: W is waiting time in ms (total time in the ready queue), T is turnaround time in ms, C is completion time, A is arrival time, b is CPU burst in ms, and S is the time the process first gets the CPU.

blocks.text: Weakness: convoy effect. With bursts 24 ms, 3 ms and 3 ms in that order, the short jobs wait 24 ms and 27 ms, average 17 ms. One long CPU-bound job at the head freezes interactive users. FCFS suits batch systems, not time-sharing.

sections.h3: Shortest job first (SJF) and shortest remaining time first

blocks.text: SJF picks the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst and runs it to completion. SRTF is its preemptive version: it compares the running process's remaining time with each new arrival and switches when the newcomer is shorter.

When all processes arrive together, SJF minimises average waiting time. If two neighbours have bursts a > b, swapping them cuts the b job's wait by a and adds only b to the a job's wait: a net gain. Repeat until bursts are sorted.

blocks.where: τₙ₊₁ is the predicted next burst in ms, tₙ is the last actual burst in ms, τₙ is the prediction made for that burst in ms, and α is a weight with 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.

blocks.text: The next burst is unknown, so predict it by this exponential average. α = 0 ignores recent history; α = 1 uses only the last burst; α = 1/2 is common. Old bursts get weights α(1−α), α(1−α)², and so on, which shrink fast. SJF gives average wait 3 ms in the example against 17 ms for FCFS, but short jobs can starve a long one.

Priority scheduling stores a priority number in each PCB and runs the highest-priority ready process. Most textbooks let a small number mean high priority, so priority 1 beats 10. State your convention.
Priorities may be internal, derived by the OS from memory need, time limit or burst ratio, or external, set by user importance or the department paying.

Preemptive priority switches on a higher-priority arrival; non-preemptive priority waits for the running process to finish. Starvation is possible: low-priority work may wait forever. Aging raises a waiting process's priority by one step every so often, so it eventually outranks newcomers.
Priority inversion: a high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task that a medium-priority task keeps preempting. Unit 3 covers the fix.

Round robin (RR) is FCFS with a clock. Each process gets a time quantum q, typically 10–100 ms. When q expires, a timer interrupt preempts the process, puts it at the tail of the circular ready queue, and the head runs. RR is always preemptive.

Two extremes. If q exceeds every burst, nothing is preempted and RR behaves like FCFS. If q is tiny, context switches dominate. With q = 1 ms and a switch costing 10 µs, overhead is about 1%. At q = 10 µs with a 10 µs switch, half the CPU time goes into switching; the overhead fraction is s/(q + s), which approaches 1 as q shrinks. Pick q large enough for most bursts and far larger than the switch time.
RR does not minimise average waiting time; it minimises response time and shares the CPU fairly. In the example its average wait is 5.67 ms, between SJF's 3 ms and FCFS's 17 ms.

Real schedulers combine rules. A multilevel queue gives each class its own queue and algorithm: interactive work in RR, batch work in FCFS. A multilevel feedback queue moves CPU-hungry processes to lower queues with longer quanta; aging lifts them back. Linux CFS keeps one run queue and picks the task with the smallest virtual runtime, an idea from fair queueing rather than the queue ladder (Chapter 2.9); the multilevel feedback queue is the Windows-style relative.

figure.caption: Jobs of 24, 3 and 3 ms, all arriving at 0, under three rules: FCFS makes the short jobs wait behind the long one (17 ms average), SJF runs them first (3 ms), and round robin with q = 4 ms sits between (17/3 ≈ 5.67 ms).

spec.aria: Three Gantt charts from 0 to 30 ms for FCFS, shortest job first and round robin with a 4 ms quantum, each labelled with its average waiting time.

examples.question: Three processes P1, P2 and P3 all arrive at time 0 in that order, with CPU bursts 24 ms, 3 ms and 3 ms. Draw the Gantt chart and find the average waiting time under (a) FCFS, (b) non-preemptive SJF, (c) round robin with q = 4 ms.
steps: FCFS runs P1 0–24 ms, P2 24–27 ms, P3 27–30 ms. Arrival is 0, so W = start. Waits are 0, 24 and 27 ms; average 17 ms. Turnaround times are 24, 27 and 30 ms; average 27 ms.
SJF runs P2 0–3 ms, P3 3–6 ms, P1 6–30 ms. Waits are 0, 3 and 6 ms; average 3 ms. Turnaround times are 3, 6 and 30 ms; average 13 ms.
RR q = 4 ms: P1 runs 0–4 ms with 20 ms left and joins the tail. Queue is P2, P3, P1. P2 runs 4–7 ms and finishes. P3 runs 7–10 ms and finishes.
P1 gets slices 10–14, 14–18, 18–22, 22–26 and 26–30 ms and finishes.
Completion times: P1 = 30 ms, P2 = 7 ms, P3 = 10 ms. W = C − A − b: 30−24 = 6 ms, 7−3 = 4 ms, 10−3 = 7 ms.
Average W for RR = (6 + 4 + 7) / 3 = 17 / 3 ≈ 5.67 ms. SJF is best, RR is in the middle, FCFS is worst; RR gives short jobs a first response at 4 ms and 7 ms.
examples.answer: Average waiting times are 17 ms for FCFS, 3 ms for SJF and 17/3 ≈ 5.67 ms for round robin with q = 4 ms.

from collections import deque
burst={'P1':24,'P2':3,'P3':3}; order=['P1','P2','P3']; n=3
t=0; w={}
for p in order: w[p]=t; t+=burst[p]
print(round(sum(w.values())/n,2))
t=0; w={}
for p in sorted(order,key=lambda x:(burst[x],order.index(x))): w[p]=t; t+=burst[p]
print(round(sum(w.values())/n,2))
q=4; rem=dict(burst); Q=deque(order); fin={}; t=0
while Q:
 p=Q.popleft(); r=min(q,rem[p]); t+=r; rem[p]-=r
 if rem[p]==0: fin[p]=t
 else: Q.append(p)
print(round(sum(fin[p]-burst[p] for p in order)/n,2))

traps: Different arrival times: when CPU idle, choose only arrived processes. SRTF preempts only for strictly shorter new arrival. Draw timeline.

Waiting is not turnaround. Use W = C − A − b; T = C − A = W + b. The short form W = S − A holds only when the process runs from first dispatch to completion without preemption (FCFS, non-preemptive SJF, non-preemptive priority).
State priority convention. Smaller number usually means higher priority; follow the question if reversed.
RR bookkeeping: preempted process joins tail behind arrivals during its slice; last slice may be shorter than q.
Large q makes RR like FCFS; tiny q makes switch overhead dominate. RR does not minimise average waiting time.

quiz.q: State the rule FCFS uses to pick the next process and name its main weakness.
quiz.a: It takes the process that has been in the ready queue longest (FIFO) and runs it to completion. Weakness: the convoy effect, where one long job delays every short job behind it.

quiz.q: Why does SJF give the minimum average waiting time when all processes arrive together?
quiz.a: If two neighbours have bursts a > b, swapping them lowers the b job's wait by a and raises the a job's wait only by b, a net gain. Repeating removes all inversions, leaving bursts sorted, which is SJF.

quiz.q: P1, P2, P3, P4 arrive at time 0 with bursts 6 ms, 8 ms, 7 ms and 3 ms. Find the average waiting time for FCFS in the stated order and for SJF.
quiz.a: FCFS starts are 0, 6, 14, 21 ms; waits 0, 6, 14, 21; average 41/4 = 10.25 ms. SJF order P4, P1, P3, P2: starts 0, 3, 9, 16 ms; waits 0, 3, 9, 16; average 28/4 = 7 ms.

quiz.q: A process was predicted to need τ₁ = 10 ms. Its actual bursts are 12 ms and then 8 ms, with α = 0.5. Find τ₂ and τ₃.
What happens to round robin when q becomes larger than every burst, and when q becomes smaller than the context-switch time?
quiz.a: With q larger than every burst no process is preempted, so RR becomes FCFS. With q smaller than the switch time, most CPU time goes into saving and restoring state, so useful throughput collapses.

quiz.q: What is aging and which problem does it solve?
quiz.a: Aging gradually raises the priority of a process that has waited a long time. It prevents starvation in priority scheduling, so a low-priority process eventually gets the CPU.

quiz.q: An interactive desktop runs short jobs beside one long compile. Explain why a multilevel feedback queue suits this workload better than plain FCFS or plain SJF.
quiz.a: FCFS lets the compile block short jobs. SJF needs burst predictions and can starve the compile. A multilevel feedback queue runs new short jobs in a high-priority small-quantum queue for fast response, and pushes the CPU-heavy compile to a lower queue with a longer quantum, with aging to stop starvation.

beyond: Not for exam. Linux CFS's virtual-runtime pick is being replaced by EEVDF-style lag tracking, so a task cheated earlier is paid back later. Kubernetes uses priority classes, preemption and fairness at pod level. Cloud batch systems add deadline and cost as criteria. Search EEVDF, Windows multilevel feedback queue, and real-time scheduling in Chapter 2.8.
